name: game payment and web shop platforms
title: Best Game Payment and Web Shop Platforms in 2026
summary_line: Compare platforms that let game studios sell in-game items and games through their own web stores, with tax, payments and merchant of record handled.
definition: A game payment and web shop platform lets a studio sell items, currency or games to players outside the app stores. It hosts the web store and checkout, accepts local payment methods, and in many cases acts as merchant of record, taking over sales tax, VAT, fraud handling and chargebacks so the studio does not register in each market itself.
intro: Studios that sell directly to players have two jobs that look alike but are not: building a storefront players want to open, and taking money in dozens of countries without becoming a tax department. The vendors below split along that line. Some are built for games and ship web shops, offers and launchers. Others are general payment or merchant of record companies that list games as one use case. We read each vendor's homepage, about page and pricing page, noted what each says about payment methods, currencies, merchant of record status and fees, and weighed fit for an indie or mid-size studio rather than a platform holder. We did not run transactions. Where a figure comes from the vendor, the entry says so, and where no price is shown we say that the vendor sells on quote or through a contact form. Thirteen vendors passed the check; one planned vendor could not be opened and was dropped.

criteria.heading: Who carries the tax and chargeback burden
criteria.text: A web shop is only cheaper than a store cut if you do not rebuild compliance yourself. Check whether the vendor names itself merchant of record, because that is the sentence that moves sales tax, VAT and most fraud exposure off your books. Platforms that only process payments leave registration, remittance and disputes with you. Several vendors on this page offer both modes, so read which product you would actually be buying. Pay particular attention to chargeback handling and to whether tax is calculated per country or per region.

criteria.heading: Reach in payment methods and currencies
criteria.text: Players in Southeast Asia, Brazil or Turkey rarely pay by card. A shop that lists many local methods and currencies converts better in those markets than one that stops at cards and wallets. Vendors quote counts such as 130+ currencies or 1000+ methods; treat those as vendor claims and compare the ones that matter for your audience, including carrier billing and prepaid vouchers. Also ask whether prices can be set per region, since a single dollar price loses sales in cheaper markets.

criteria.heading: Storefront and live-ops tools
criteria.text: Some platforms hand you a payment page; others give you a branded store, personalized offers, loyalty rewards, a launcher or deep links from inside the game. If your live-ops team already runs offers, a plain checkout may be enough. If not, built-in offer logic and player segmentation save engineering time. Look at how the shop connects to the game: SDK, link-out, payment links or server calls, and who owns the player identity during purchase.

criteria.heading: Fee transparency and contract terms
criteria.text: Most game-focused vendors do not print their rates. Expect a contact form, a demo request or a performance-based fee. That is workable, but it means your first real comparison happens in a sales call, so go in with your expected monthly volume and average purchase size. A published rate card, volume discounts, minimums, payout schedules and exit terms all belong on your question list. Be wary of any claim about what you keep per sale until the fee basis is written down.

market_notes: The list splits into two camps. Seven vendors are built around games or digital goods: Xsolla, Appcharge, Coda Payments, Stash, Aghanim, Tebex and Boku. The other six are general merchants or payment processors: FastSpring, Paddle, Paymentwall, Nuvei, Adyen and Stripe. Among the pages we read, only Coda prints percentage rates, 1%, 5% and a flat 15% per transaction, and Adyen describes its structure without figures. At least eight of the thirteen route pricing questions to a contact form, a demo or a sales call.

The main trade-off is control against effort. A merchant of record that also builds the store, such as Appcharge or Stash, shortens launch time but ties your offer logic to one vendor. A processor such as Adyen or Stripe gives you the rails and leaves tax, shop design and fraud policy to you. Two vendors, Appcharge and Aghanim, focus on mobile games specifically, which matters because link-out from an app has different rules from a PC storefront. Several of the figures above, such as volume processed or countries covered, are vendor-reported and not independently confirmed.

how_to_choose.title: Decide who stays merchant of record
how_to_choose.text: Write down whether you want tax and compliance taken off your hands or whether you already have an entity set up for it. If the answer is take it off, shortlist only vendors that state merchant of record on their own pages: Xsolla, Appcharge, Stash, Aghanim, Coda Payments, FastSpring and Paddle are the ones whose opened pages say so or describe it. If you already handle tax through a finance team, a processor may cost less and give you more control.

how_to_choose.title: Match the platform to where players are
how_to_choose.text: List your top five player countries and the payment methods people use there. Then check each vendor's stated coverage for exactly those markets, not the global headline number. A shop that reaches 200+ countries on paper may still lack the voucher or wallet your biggest market prefers. Ask for the method list by country in writing before you sign anything, and test a checkout from a device located in that market if a demo store is available.

how_to_choose.title: Price it with your own numbers
how_to_choose.text: Take your last full month of sales, split by country and average purchase value, and ask two or three vendors to quote against it. Compare total cost including tax handling, refunds, chargebacks and payout fees, not only the headline rate. For vendors that publish rates, like Coda, check which rate applies to your volume tier. For quote-only vendors, push for a written rate card and a minimum term before you commit engineering time to an integration.

faqs.q: What is the best game payment and web shop platform in 2026?
faqs.a: Xsolla is the broadest fit: a games-first company with web shop, payments and publishing tools, covering 200+ geographies and 1000+ payment methods according to its About page. Appcharge is the better pick if you ship a mobile game and want a branded web store with merchant of record. Coda Payments is the better pick if you want published per-transaction rates.

faqs.q: Do I need a merchant of record to sell in-game items on the web?
faqs.a: You do not strictly need one, but without it you register for sales tax and VAT where required, remit it, and handle disputes yourself. A merchant of record becomes the seller of record to the player and takes on that work for a fee. Small studios usually choose one to avoid building a compliance function.

faqs.q: How much does a game web shop platform cost?
faqs.a: It depends on the vendor, and most do not print rates. Coda lists standard rates from 1% to 15% per transaction on its pricing page, with custom pricing from $100K USD monthly volume. Xsolla, Appcharge, Stash and Tebex direct buyers to sales contacts. Adyen charges a fixed fee plus a payment-method fee with no setup cost.

faqs.q: Can a web shop replace app store billing for a mobile game?
faqs.a: It can supplement it. Vendors such as Appcharge and Aghanim sell in-game items through web stores reached by links from the game. Whether you may steer players off the store depends on platform rules in each region, which change, so confirm the current terms for each store before moving volume.

faqs.q: Which platforms suit a PC or console studio rather than mobile?
faqs.a: Xsolla describes web shops for mobile, PC and web games, and Tebex serves server-based games and webstores. FastSpring lists a video games use case for selling games direct to consumers, and Paddle's use-case pages cover games alongside SaaS. Appcharge and Aghanim describe a mobile focus.

faqs.q: Is Stripe enough for a small game studio?
faqs.a: Stripe is enough if you only need to accept payments and are comfortable running tax and your own store pages. Its opened pages describe payments, billing, invoicing and tax tools, with 135+ currencies and payment methods. It does not provide a games-specific web shop, offers or launcher, so expect more build work than with a games-first platform.

faqs.q: What is carrier billing and does it matter for games?
faqs.a: Carrier billing charges a purchase to a phone bill, which helps in markets where players lack cards. Boku builds around local payment methods including wallets and direct carrier billing, and states 200+ local methods in 40+ markets on its homepage. It matters most if a large share of your audience is in prepaid mobile markets.

tools.name: Xsolla
tools.tagline: Games-first commerce suite with web shop and payments
tools.pricing: Not stated on the opened pages; the pricing URL leads to a contact form, and the homepage says tools launch with no upfront costs.
tools.platforms: Web shop for mobile, PC and web games
tools.summary: Ranks first because it is the only vendor here that pairs a games-specific web shop with payments, publishing and live-ops tooling under one roof.
tools.verdict: Xsolla calls itself the global video game commerce company, and the opened pages back that with a product range that goes past checkout: Web Shop, Xsolla Pay, a Publishing Suite, an SDK and LiveOps. The About page cites 200+ geographies, 1000+ payment methods and 130+ currencies, and the homepage says Web Shop lets studios keep up to 95% of each sale. Those are vendor figures, but they describe the widest reach among the vendors we read, which suits a studio selling across PC, mobile and web.
tools.weaknesses: No rate card is shown; the pricing link ends at a contact form, so the up to 95% claim cannot be checked against fees before a sales call. The breadth also means more products to evaluate than a studio needing only a checkout page.
tools.wrong_for: Skip it if you want a published rate card up front or a plain card processor. Look at Coda Payments for printed rates or Stripe for bare payment rails.

tools.wrong_for: Not for PC or console studios, who should look at Xsolla or Tebex. Teams that want fees printed in advance should check Coda Payments.

tools.name: Coda Payments
tools.tagline: Webstore, link-out payments and merchant of record with listed rates
tools.pricing: Standard rates start from 1% per transaction, with other standard rates of 5% and a flat 15% per transaction; custom pricing for companies expecting at least $100K USD of volume per month.
tools.summary: Third because it is the one games-focused vendor that prints per-transaction rates and still offers a webstore and merchant of record.
tools.verdict: The Coda pricing page is the most concrete of any games-focused vendor in this list. It shows three standard rates, from 1% up to a flat 15% per transaction, and moves to custom pricing once a company expects $100K USD of monthly volume. Around that sits a webstore, link-out payments through Coda Links and a merchant of record offer. The homepage adds that Coda reaches more than 380 million consumers through its own platforms. A studio can estimate cost before talking to sales.
tools.weaknesses: The pricing page does not say which product each of the three rates applies to in the text we read, so you still need to ask what 1% versus 15% buys. The 380 million reach figure is a vendor claim.
tools.wrong_for: Large publishers with bespoke contracts will outgrow the standard tiers; compare Xsolla or Nuvei. Studios wanting a heavily personalized store should see Appcharge.

tools.summary: Fourth because it bundles a webshop, launcher and loyalty program with merchant of record, but gives less on payment coverage and price.

tools.wrong_for: Studios judging vendors by payment-method breadth should compare Xsolla or Appcharge. Those wanting printed rates should read Coda Payments.

tools.verdict: Aghanim combines a billing engine, merchant of record and player incentive tools for mobile games. The company is Aghanim, Inc., with headquarters in Los Angeles and a tech hub in Lisbon according to the homepage, and the founders are listed as former executives of Xsolla and Xsolla Labs. tools.wrong_for: PC and console studios should not start here; Tebex or Xsolla fit better. Teams that need published numbers on method coverage should look at Boku or Paymentwall.

tools.name: Tebex
tools.tagline: Webstores, checkout and store protection for game servers and studios
tools.pricing: Not stated on the page; the site offers Talk to sales and Open Account buttons.
tools.summary: Sixth because it has the largest self-reported merchant base and a store-protection product, but the pages show less detail on tax handling.
tools.verdict: Tebex describes itself as the extension that carries the operational complexity behind game monetization, with Webstores, Checkout and Store Protection in the menu. The homepage states $1.5B processed, 45K+ businesses monetizing, 130+ payment methods and 70+ countries, all vendor figures. The Open Account button suggests a lower-friction start than a sales-gated vendor, and the server monetization angle fits games where community operators sell perks. It is the sensible look for server-based titles.
tools.weaknesses: The homepage does not say whether Tebex acts as merchant of record, and shows no fees. The volume figures are self-reported, and the product list is shorter than Xsolla's on live-ops and publishing.
tools.wrong_for: Mobile publishers wanting in-app link-out offers should look at Appcharge. Anyone who needs explicit merchant of record wording should check Paddle or FastSpring.

The homepage lists a Video Games use case for selling games or in-game items direct to consumers. It suits a studio selling a premium PC game or a software-style product from its own site.

tools.pricing: The pricing page says it shows Paddle's fees and offers a custom enterprise quote; the fee figures are not in the captured page text.

tools.verdict: Paddle calls its product the only complete merchant of record solution purpose-built for SaaS and apps, and games appear on its use-case pages. The feature list covers checkout, subscriptions, tax and compliance, invoicing, fraud protection and retention tools, which works well when a game is sold as a subscription, a launcher service or a mod platform. The homepage names Nexus Mods and HubX as customer stories. For a studio running a membership model rather than item shops, it is a reasonable base.
tools.weaknesses: The positioning is SaaS and apps first, with no in-game item shop, offers engine or launcher. The pricing page shows fees, but the figures were not captured in the text we read, so we cannot state them here.
tools.wrong_for: Item-shop free-to-play titles need a games-first store such as Xsolla or Stash. Studios that want a card-and-wallet processor only should compare Stripe.

tools.best_for: Studios building their own store on local methods
tools.pricing: Not stated on the opened pages; the site invites a consultation.
tools.summary: Ninth because local-method coverage is wide and plugins exist, but it is a payment provider rather than a game store.

Its products are Brick for cards, PayAlto for local methods, a Gateway, eInvoicing, Passport and Subscriptions, and the homepage says more than 150 local methods are reachable through one API. Plugins are listed for Shopify, WooCommerce and Magento, so a studio that already runs a web shop on one of those can add local methods. San Francisco is its Global HQ per the About page.
tools.weaknesses: No game-specific storefront, offers or launcher is described, and merchant-of-record status is not stated on the pages we opened. Pricing is by consultation only, so cost is unknown.
tools.wrong_for: Studios without engineering time for a custom store should pick Appcharge or Xsolla. Anyone who needs a stated tax-handling model should look at FastSpring.

tools.name: Nuvei
tools.tagline: Global payments infrastructure with gaming use cases
tools.best_for: Large publishers with in-house payments teams
tools.pricing: Not stated on the page; merchants are directed to contact sales.
tools.summary: Eleventh because the infrastructure is deep, with over 720 payment options and gaming use cases, but it targets larger teams and publishes no price.
tools.verdict: Nuvei calls itself the infrastructure for every payment, everywhere, and its Who we are page presents it as a global payments infrastructure provider. The feature list spans pay-ins, payouts, global acquiring, fraud and risk management, chargeback resolution and payment orchestration. The homepage says over 720 payment options and lists use cases for online gaming and video gaming monetization. A publisher with a payments team that wants to route across processors will see more here than in a store-in-a-box product.
tools.weaknesses: It does not ship a games web shop or offers engine, and it directs merchants to contact sales for any price. The breadth of payments infrastructure is more than a small studio needs.
tools.wrong_for: Indie studios without a payments engineer should not start here; Coda Payments or Appcharge hand over a finished store. Teams wanting stated fees should see Adyen.

tools.name: Adyen
tools.tagline: Enterprise payments platform billed per transaction
tools.best_for: Large studios running their own checkout
tools.pricing: Pay per transaction with no setup or monthly fees: a fixed processing fee plus a fee set by the payment method, per the pricing page.
tools.summary: Twelfth because the fee structure is stated and coverage is wide, yet it is an enterprise processor and leaves store, tax and compliance to you.
tools.verdict: Adyen describes itself as a fintech platform for enterprises that runs payments, data and financial products on one platform. The pricing page is plain: a fixed processing fee plus a fee set by the payment method, with no setup or monthly fees. The homepage states 150+ currencies and 200+ local payment methods. For a large studio with its own storefront and finance team, that structure is easy to model, and Aghanim's announced partnership with Adyen shows games platforms build on it.
tools.weaknesses: It provides no games web shop, offers or merchant-of-record service in the pages we opened, so tax, fraud policy and store design stay with you. Enterprise positioning makes onboarding heavier for small studios.
tools.wrong_for: Small studios that want a hosted store should pick Appcharge or Stash. Teams wanting a simple developer-first API may find Stripe quicker.
